questions.title: A descending projectile
questions.stem: A projectile is launched with horizontal and upward velocity components $8.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $6.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Air resistance is negligible; use $g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. At what horizontal distance is it at height $1.6\,\mathrm{m}$ while descending?
questions.changeNotes: New numerical data and a changed inference or linked modelling task; original wording and recomputed distractors.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Link physical models, interpret conditions and justify the result.

verification.method: Author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: See the named reproducible author checks and worked solution for this question.

steps.text: Solve $1.6=6t-5t^2$ to obtain $t=0.40$ or $0.80\,\mathrm{s}$. Since $v_y=6-10t$, descent occurs at $0.80\,\mathrm{s}$. Thus $x=8(0.80)=6.4\,\mathrm{m}$. The smaller root is the upward crossing. Therefore choose A.

questions.title: Direction-dependent drag
questions.stem: Two identical balls in separate trials pass a chosen height with equal speeds, one moving upward and the other downward. At this speed each ball has drag magnitude $0.40mg$. What is the ratio of the upward-moving ball's acceleration magnitude to the downward-moving ball's acceleration magnitude?

sourceAnchors.focus: Air resistance and acceleration on ascent/descent

questions.changeNotes: New numerical data and a changed inference or linked modelling task; original wording and recomputed distractors.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Link physical models, interpret conditions and justify the result.

verification.method: Author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: See the named reproducible author checks and worked solution for this question.

steps.text: On ascent, weight and drag both act down, giving $1.40g$. On descent, drag acts up, giving $0.60g$ down. The ratio is $1.40/0.60=7/3$. Equal speeds give equal drag magnitudes, not equal resultant forces. Therefore choose C.

After a collision Y moves right at $5.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. How much total kinetic energy is dissipated?

steps.text: Taking right positive, $2(6)+1(-3)=2v_X+1(5)$, so $v_X=2.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Initial kinetic energy is $40.5\,\mathrm{J}$ and final is $16.5\,\mathrm{J}$, giving $24\,\mathrm{J}$ dissipated. Momentum needs signed velocities; kinetic energy needs squared speeds. Therefore choose B.

questions.title: Spring energy between extensions
questions.stem: A spring obeys Hooke's law. Stretching it from extension $0.040\,\mathrm{m}$ to $0.100\,\mathrm{m}$ requires $0.84\,\mathrm{J}$. What energy is stored at extension $0.080\,\mathrm{m}$, measured from its natural length?
questions.changeNotes: New numerical data and a changed inference or linked modelling task; original wording and recomputed distractors.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Link physical models, interpret conditions and justify the result.

verification.method: Author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: See the named reproducible author checks and worked solution for this question.

steps.text: Use $0.84=\tfrac12 k(0.100^2-0.040^2)$, giving $k=200\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$. Then $E=\tfrac12(200)(0.080)^2=0.64\,\mathrm{J}$. Work between extensions is a difference of squares, not the square of their difference. Therefore choose C.

questions.title: Thermal equilibrium
questions.stem: An insulated container mixes $0.30\,\mathrm{kg}$ of liquid P at $10^\circ\mathrm{C}$ with $0.20\,\mathrm{kg}$ of liquid Q at $70^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The final temperature is $30^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Heat absorbed by the container is negligible. What is $c_P/c_Q$?

steps.text: Energy conservation gives $0.30c_P(30-10)=0.20c_Q(70-30)$. Thus $c_P/c_Q=8/6=4/3$. The different masses as well as the temperature changes must be included. Therefore choose D.

questions.title: Albedo and emissivity
questions.stem: Surfaces X and Y have the same temperature. X receives $400\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, reflects $80\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ and emits $300\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ as infrared. Y receives $600\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, reflects $180\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ and emits $200\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. Which statement follows?

sourceAnchors.focus: Separate definitions of albedo and emissivity

questions.changeNotes: New numerical data and a changed inference or linked modelling task; original wording and recomputed distractors.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Link physical models, interpret conditions and justify the result.

verification.method: Author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: See the named reproducible author checks and worked solution for this question.

options.label: A
options.text: X has the greater albedo and $\varepsilon_X/\varepsilon_Y=2/3$.

options.label: B
options.text: Y has the greater albedo and $\varepsilon_X/\varepsilon_Y=2/3$.

options.label: C
options.text: Y has the greater albedo and $\varepsilon_X/\varepsilon_Y=1.50$.

options.label: D
options.text: X has the greater albedo and $\varepsilon_X/\varepsilon_Y=1.50$.

steps.text: Albedo is reflected divided by incident intensity: $0.20$ for X and $0.30$ for Y. At equal temperature, emitted intensity is proportional to emissivity, so $\varepsilon_X/\varepsilon_Y=300/200=1.50$. These data need not describe thermal equilibrium. Therefore choose C.

questions.answerSummary: C: Y has the greater albedo and $\varepsilon_X/\varepsilon_Y=1.50$.

An increase in infrared-absorbing gas initially reduces the outgoing intensity to $180\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, without changing absorbed sunlight. Which prediction is consistent with energy conservation?

options.label: A
options.text: The gas permanently removes $60\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ of energy from the universe.

options.label: B
options.text: The planet initially loses energy and cools until it emits $180\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$.

options.label: C
options.text: The planet remains at the same temperature because incoming sunlight is unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: The planet initially gains energy, and warming can restore outgoing intensity to $240\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$.

steps.text: Initially the gain is $240-180=60\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. Infrared absorption and re-emission redistribute energy; they do not destroy it. A higher planetary temperature can increase emission until the top-of-atmosphere balance is restored. Therefore choose D.

questions.answerSummary: D: The planet initially gains energy, and warming can restore outgoing intensity to $240\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$.

questions.title: Microscopic gas comparisons
questions.stem: Two monatomic ideal-gas samples have the same temperature. Sample X contains twice as many atoms as sample Y, and each X atom has one-fifth the mass of a Y atom. What are $U_X/U_Y$ and $v_{\rm rms,X}/v_{\rm rms,Y}$?

sourceAnchors.focus: Molecular mass, number and internal energy

questions.changeNotes: New numerical data and a changed inference or linked modelling task; original wording and recomputed distractors.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Link physical models, interpret conditions and justify the result.

verification.method: Author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: See the named reproducible author checks and worked solution for this question.

steps.text: For a monatomic ideal gas $U=\tfrac32Nk_BT$, so the energy ratio is $2$. Also $\tfrac12m\langle v^2\rangle=\tfrac32k_BT$, so the rms speed ratio is $\sqrt{m_Y/m_X}=\sqrt5$. Atom number does not set the rms speed at fixed temperature. Therefore choose B.

options.text: Interference disappears because the frequencies are now different.

options.label: D
options.text: Constructive interference changes to destructive interference.

steps.text: The path difference is $0.60\,\mathrm{m}=1.5\lambda$, so initially the waves arrive half a cycle out of phase. An additional half-cycle source shift makes the arrival phase difference a whole number of cycles, giving constructive interference. A fixed phase shift does not change frequency or coherence. Therefore choose A.

questions.answerSummary: A: Destructive interference changes to constructive interference.

steps.text: Successive allowed modes of an open-closed tube differ in length by $\lambda/2$. Hence $\lambda=2(0.540-0.180)=0.720\,\mathrm{m}$ and $f=343/0.720=476\,\mathrm{Hz}$. Subtraction cancels the constant end correction. Therefore choose B.

questions.title: Resonance width
questions.stem: The solid and dashed curves show the steady-state displacement amplitude of the same driven oscillator under two damping conditions. The driving-force amplitude is unchanged. Which conclusion is supported?
questions.changeNotes: New numerical data and a changed inference or linked modelling task; original wording and recomputed distractors.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Link physical models, interpret conditions and justify the result.

verification.method: Author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: See the named reproducible author checks and worked solution for this question.

options.label: A
options.text: The dashed response has greater damping and a broader, lower resonance peak.

options.label: B
options.text: The dashed response has less damping and a broader, lower resonance peak.

options.label: C
options.text: The solid response has greater damping because its peak is taller.

options.label: D
options.text: The natural frequency must double when damping is increased.

steps.text: Increased damping dissipates more energy per cycle and reduces the build-up of amplitude near resonance. Its response is lower and broader. A taller peak is a sign of less damping, and the data do not imply a doubled natural frequency. Therefore choose A.

questions.answerSummary: A: The dashed response has greater damping and a broader, lower resonance peak.

questions.title: Comparing orbital systems
questions.stem: A planet follows a circular orbit of radius $r$ and period $T$ about star X. Another planet orbits star Y with radius $2r$ and period $T/2$. Planet masses are negligible. What is $M_Y/M_X$?
questions.changeNotes: New numerical data and a changed inference or linked modelling task; original wording and recomputed distractors.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Link physical models, interpret conditions and justify the result.

verification.method: Author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: See the named reproducible author checks and worked solution for this question.

steps.text: From $T^2=4\pi^2r^3/(GM)$, stellar mass is proportional to $r^3/T^2$. The ratio is $2^3/(1/2)^2=32$. The two planets orbit different stars, so one cannot use a constant $T^2/r^3$ for both without accounting for mass. Therefore choose B.

questions.title: A velocity selector and a magnetic analyser
questions.subtopic: A velocity selector and a magnetic analyser
questions.stem: A particle of mass $m$ and positive charge $q$ passes undeflected through crossed fields, then enters a region containing only the same magnetic field, following radius $r$. A second particle has mass $2m$ and charge $q/2$. It also passes undeflected through the selector. What is its analyser radius?

sourceAnchors.focus: Crossed-field selection followed by circular motion

steps.text: Undeflected motion requires $qE=qvB$, so both selected particles have $v=E/B$, independent of mass and charge. In the magnetic-only region $r=mv/(qB)$. The second ratio is $(2m)/(q/2)$ divided by $m/q$, giving $4r$. Therefore choose D.

questions.title: Testing the nuclear model
questions.stem: A very thin metal foil produces a small number of large-angle alpha-particle deflections. Which observation most directly supports concentration of positive charge in a very small nucleus?

verification.method: Author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks

options.label: A
options.text: All incident particles turn back from the foil surface.

options.label: B
options.text: A tiny fraction of incident particles reverse direction, while most pass nearly straight through.

options.label: C
options.text: Every incident particle loses exactly the same fraction of its energy.

options.label: D
options.text: The scattered particles have a continuous range of negative charges.

steps.text: Rare large-angle/backward deflections require a highly concentrated repulsive region. The near-straight passage of most particles implies that this region occupies a small fraction of atomic volume. Uniform positive charge cannot readily account for the rare strong deflections. Therefore choose B.

questions.answerSummary: B: A tiny fraction of incident particles reverse direction, while most pass nearly straight through.

questions.title: Successive nuclear transformations
questions.stem: A uranium nucleus ${}^{238}_{92}\mathrm U$ undergoes alpha decay. Its daughter subsequently undergoes beta-minus decay. What are the final nucleon number and proton number?

sourceAnchors.focus: Conservation of nucleon number and charge

questions.changeNotes: New numerical data and a changed inference or linked modelling task; original wording and recomputed distractors.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Link physical models, interpret conditions and justify the result.

verification.method: Author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: See the named reproducible author checks and worked solution for this question.

steps.text: Alpha decay reduces nucleon number by $4$ and proton number by $2$, yielding $A=234,Z=90$. Beta-minus changes a neutron into a proton, leaving $A$ unchanged and increasing $Z$ to $91$. The emitted electron is not a pre-existing orbital electron. Therefore choose C.

questions.title: Background-corrected decay
questions.stem: A source has half-life $40\,\mathrm{s}$. A detector measures $116\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ at $t=0$ and $44\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ at $t=80\,\mathrm{s}$. Background is constant. What is the ratio of source count rate to background count rate at $t=120\,\mathrm{s}$?

sourceAnchors.focus: Infer background before using integer half-lives

questions.changeNotes: New numerical data and a changed inference or linked modelling task; original wording and recomputed distractors.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Link physical models, interpret conditions and justify the result.

verification.method: Author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: See the named reproducible author checks and worked solution for this question.

steps.text: Let background be $b$. Two half-lives give $44-b=(116-b)/4$, hence $b=20\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. After three half-lives the source contributes $(116-20)/8=12\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The requested ratio is $12/20=0.60$, using source rather than gross rate. Therefore choose D.

questions.title: Binding energy in fission
questions.stem: A uranium-235 nucleus captures one neutron and splits into nuclei with nucleon numbers $141$ and $92$, plus free neutrons. Binding energy per nucleon is $7.6\,\mathrm{MeV}$ for uranium, $8.4\,\mathrm{MeV}$ for the first fragment and $8.6\,\mathrm{MeV}$ for the second. Approximately how much energy is released?
questions.changeNotes: New numerical data and a changed inference or linked modelling task; original wording and recomputed distractors.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Link physical models, interpret conditions and justify the result.

verification.method: Author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: See the named reproducible author checks and worked solution for this question.

steps.text: Free neutrons have zero nuclear binding energy. Total final binding is $141(8.4)+92(8.6)=1975.6\,\mathrm{MeV}$; initial binding is $235(7.6)=1786.0\,\mathrm{MeV}$. The increase, $189.6\,\mathrm{MeV}$, is released. Conservation also gives three free neutrons. Therefore choose A.

steps.text: The full six-month angular displacement is twice the parallax angle. Thus $p=0.0500$ arc-seconds, $d=1/p=20.0\,\mathrm{pc}$, and $d=65.2\,\mathrm{ly}$. Using the full displacement as $p$ produces a factor-of-two error. Therefore choose C.

questions.title: An oscillating pen on an accelerating cart
questions.subtopic: An oscillating pen on an accelerating cart
questions.stem:
A pen attached to a cart oscillates perpendicular to the direction of travel. Its calibrated frequency is $(10.0\pm0.2)\,\mathrm{Hz}$. The trace records successive positive peaks at the longitudinal positions below. Each position has maximum uncertainty $0.001\,\mathrm m$. Treat the frequency uncertainty as a maximum uncertainty and use a constant-acceleration model.

| Peak number | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Position / m | 0.000 | 0.020 | 0.044 | 0.072 | 0.104 | 0.140 |

sourceAnchors.focus: Cart motion recorded by an oscillating pen

questions.changeNotes: Rebuilt context/data and part sequence with independently recomputed results and a new precise figure where useful.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Link physical models, interpret conditions and justify the result.

verification.method: Author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: See the named reproducible author checks and worked solution for this question.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the time between successive peaks and its maximum uncertainty.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Estimate the longitudinal velocity at peak 2 using peaks 1 and 3.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Use the change in successive peak spacings to determine the acceleration.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Calculate the maximum uncertainty in your velocity estimate in (b).

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: A student says that increasing longitudinal peak spacings prove the pen frequency is increasing. Evaluate this claim.

steps.text: $\delta T/T=\delta f/f=0.020$, giving $\delta T=0.002\,\mathrm s$.
Use the central interval: $v\approx(x_3-x_1)/(2T)$.
$v=(0.072-0.020)/0.200=0.260\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. For constant acceleration, this is the instantaneous velocity at the midpoint time.
Successive spacings increase by $0.004\,\mathrm m$. With equal time intervals, $\Delta(\Delta x)=aT^2$.
$\delta(\Delta x)=0.002\,\mathrm m$ and $\delta(2T)=0.004\,\mathrm s$. Add fractional maximum uncertainties: $\delta v/v=0.002/0.052+0.004/0.200$.
$\delta v=0.0152\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so $v=(0.260\pm0.015)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; accept sensible uncertainty rounding such as $0.26\pm0.02$.
The calibration gives a constant time between peaks; increasing spatial spacing can result from increasing cart speed.
The trace alone does not demonstrate a frequency increase. A separate time calibration is needed; the constant-frequency accelerating-cart model is consistent with the data.

questions.answerSummary: (a) $\delta T/T=\delta f/f=0.020$, giving $\delta T=0.002\,\mathrm s$.; (b) $v=(0.072-0.020)/0.200=0.260\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. For constant acceleration, this is the instantaneous velocity at the midpoint time.; (c) $a=0.004/(0.100)^2=0.400\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.; (d) $\delta v=0.0152\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so $v=(0.260\pm0.015)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; accept sensible uncertainty rounding such as $0.26\pm0.02$.; (e) The trace alone does not demonstrate a frequency increase. A separate time calibration is needed; the constant-frequency accelerating-cart model is consistent with the data.

questions.title: Density from a force-depth gradient
questions.stem:
A force sensor suspends a uniform vertical object partly in a liquid. The cross-sectional area is $(4.00\pm0.08)\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2}$. Immersion depth $h$ remains below the object's total length. No part touches the vessel, surface-tension effects are negligible and the object remains stationary. The measured upward sensor force is $F$. A fit to the laboratory data gives

$$F=(2.35\pm0.02)-(3.90\pm0.15)h,$$

with $F$ in newtons and $h$ in metres. Use $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

| $h$/m | 0.00 | 0.03 | 0.06 | 0.09 | 0.12 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $F$/N | 2.35 | 2.23 | 2.12 | 2.00 | 1.88 |

questions.diagramSvg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 300" role="img"><rect x="50" y="85" width="210" height="180" fill="white" stroke="#202020" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="140" x2="260" y2="140" stroke="#202020" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="130" y="100" width="55" height="120" fill="white" stroke="#202020" stroke-width="2"/><text x="157.5" y="165" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="normal" fill="#202020">object</text><line x1="157.5" y1="35" x2="157.5" y2="100" stroke="#202020" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="100" y="10" width="115" height="28" fill="white" stroke="#202020" stroke-width="2"/><text x="157.5" y="29" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="normal" fill="#202020">force sensor</text><line x1="220" y1="140" x2="220" y2="220" stroke="#202020" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="220,220 216.495,211.71 223.505,211.71" fill="#202020"/><text x="240" y="185" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="normal" fill="#202020">h</text><text x="360" y="85" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="start" font-weight="normal" fill="#202020">stationary object</text><text x="360" y="130" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" text-anchor="start" font-weight="normal" fill="#202020">uniform cross-section</text><text x="360" y="165" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" text-anchor="start" font-weight="normal" fill="#202020">no base contact</text></svg>

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the forces on the object and derive $F=W-\rho gAh$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use the gradient to determine the liquid density.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Determine the maximum uncertainty in that density. Neglect uncertainty in $g$.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Would a constant $+0.10\,\mathrm N$ force-sensor zero error change the density obtained by this method? Explain.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Explain why the straight-line model must stop applying once the object becomes completely immersed.

steps.text: Downward weight $W$ is balanced by upward sensor force and upthrust.
The displaced liquid volume is $Ah$, so upthrust is $\rho gAh$ and $F+\rho gAh=W$.
The gradient is $-\rho gA$, with magnitude $3.90\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$.
$\rho=994\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ to three significant figures.
$\delta\rho\approx58\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$; accept $(990\pm60)\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ or consistent rounding.
No. A constant force offset changes the intercept, but not the force-depth gradient, provided it is constant throughout the measurements.
Once fully immersed, the displaced volume stops increasing when the object is lowered farther.
Upthrust and sensor force then remain approximately constant for an incompressible liquid; extending the negative-gradient line would be physically wrong.

questions.answerSummary: (a) The displaced liquid volume is $Ah$, so upthrust is $\rho gAh$ and $F+\rho gAh=W$.; (b) $\rho=994\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ to three significant figures.; (c) $\delta\rho\approx58\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$; accept $(990\pm60)\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ or consistent rounding.; (d) No. A constant force offset changes the intercept, but not the force-depth gradient, provided it is constant throughout the measurements.; (e) Upthrust and sensor force then remain approximately constant for an incompressible liquid; extending the negative-gradient line would be physically wrong.
